lower court correctly assessed the violations as extremely minor. Nor is there any cause for 
objection to its consideration, in this context, that the plaintiff neither suffered any damage nor 
even began to demonstrate the existence of such damage or a risk of damage. In doing so, it by 
no means failed to recognize that the occurrence of damage is not, in principle, necessary for the 
forfeiture of the contractual penalty. Nevertheless, it was entitled to take the absence of such 
damage into account when assessing the appropriateness of the contractual penalty. This does not 
constitute a violation of the rule on the burden of proof. To the extent that the plaintiff argues 
before the Federal Supreme Court that the defendant intended to cause damage by violating the 
non-competition clause shortly after the conclusion of the purchase agreement, she has not 
substantiated this claim. Furthermore, this argument is raised out of time. When she asserts that 
several experts were confused, she relies on facts that are not relevant to the Federal Supreme 
Court.  
Likewise, the lower court correctly took into account that the breach of the non-competition 
clause occurred on only a single occasion and that there was no risk of recurrence. The plaintiff 
does not dispute this. Nor does she substantiate that the breach of the non-competition clause 
would have been “worthwhile” for the defendant—which the amount of the contractual penalty 
was intended to prevent. According to the lower court’s findings, which were not arbitrary, there 
is no evidence of this. The lower court correctly took into account that this was in fact a minor 
violation of the non-competition clause, which would not justify a contractual penalty in the 
agreed amount—even in light of the principle of good faith. The fact that the legal transaction 
underlying the non-competition clause was financially significant need not lead to a different 
conclusion. There can be no question of an arbitrary reduction of the contractual penalty that 
would be grossly contrary to the principle of fairness.  
4.3.4. Nor do the defendant’s arguments regarding the calculation of the contractual penalty 
constitute an abuse of the discretion afforded to the lower court. 
He merely repeats here that Construction21 was not engaged in any operational activities at the 
time of the letter and that no effects of the violations were apparent. The lower court also 
proceeded on this basis. It duly took into account both the minor severity of the violations and 
their effects. There is no grounds for objection to its conclusion that a contractual penalty of CHF
